newsitem.title: CHINA: China monetary policy seen easier in H2--report.
newsitem.headline: China monetary policy seen easier in H2--report.

text.p: China's monetary policy will be significantly easier in the second half of 1996 to help state firms suffering from low efficiency, weak sales and rising unemployment, the State Information Centre said in a report.
As of end-June, total outstanding loans from financial institutions were 5.438 trillion yuan, up 23.4 percent from a year earlier, the Shanghai Securities News on Sunday quoted the report as saying.

This year the central bank has twice cut bank interest rates - the last time on Thursday - and lowered the anti-inflation subsidy paid on long-term individual bank deposits, to encourage people to spend money rather than put it in the bank, it said.
But these measures have been insufficient to ease the monetary problems of state firms, so the government will take more measures to support them, especially in providing credit, it said.

Usually, new loans from state banks in the second half of the year account for 70 percent of the total of new loans for the whole year, the report said. The banks should provide an additional 400 billion yuan in new loans in the second half of 1996, it added.

It was not immediately clear how the report's expectations meshed with comments by People's Bank of China governor, Dai Xianglong, that the central bank would still keep a firm hold on monetary policy despite Thursday's reduction in bank deposit and lending rates.
"Over the next several years, we will still adopt an appropriately tight monetary policy," Dai was quoted by the China Securities newspaper on Saturday as saying.

The State Information Centre report also forecast an increase in China's trade surplus in the rest of 1996, thanks to the easier monetary policy and faster repayment of export tax rebates. It gave no further details.
